summary: Savanna and grassland animals (ages 7–9): help pupils see that OPEN grassland with few trees for cover — where animals are visible from far off — favours herding, watchfulness and speed, while seasonal rains that change where grass and water are found drive seasonal movement. The anchor cast is African savanna herbivores/plant-eaters (zebra, wildebeest, gazelle, elephant, giraffe) and predators (lion, cheetah, hyena), with American grassland parallels (bison, prairie dogs). The central, hard-to-fake idea is that grouping changes survival ODDS: in a big, alert herd many eyes spot danger early, the moving mass confuses a hunter, and each individual is less likely to be the one caught (dilution). The preferred approach lets children operate this as a probability system; alternatives (sortable scene, matching/categorisation checks, outdoor tag game, guide-in-role hook) target naming, assessment, and curiosity. Address the misconceptions that predators always win, that a big group is an easier target, that savanna is a jungle, that the fastest always wins, and that plant-eaters wander randomly.
misconceptions: 'Predators always catch their prey' — most hunts fail; prey defences and group living work often.
'Being in a big group makes you an easier target' — herding usually lowers each individual's risk (dilution, confusion, shared vigilance).
'Savanna is a jungle/forest' — it is open grassland with scattered trees, and that openness is the point.
'The fastest animal always wins' — endurance, alertness, timing and cover matter as much as top speed.
'Grazers wander randomly' — herd movements track seasonal grass and water.

activities.title: Run the hunt: a safety-in-numbers simulation
steps: Set a prey herd's size (from a lone animal up to a large herd) and how alert/watchful the animals are, then release a predator (lion or cheetah) and watch the chase play out.

Run repeated hunts and read a survival-rate meter that updates across runs, comparing a lone dozing gazelle (caught almost every time) with the same gazelle in a big, watchful herd (spotted early, the mass scatters, most hunts fail).
Make the hunt two-sided: increase the predator's speed or stamina and discover the prey must group tighter and stay more alert to keep surviving.
Use a season toggle that moves grass and water so the herd must relocate to keep feeding, connecting behaviour to seasonal migration.
activities.insight: Safety in numbers is not a slogan but a reduction in each individual's risk — from more eyes watching, confusion of a moving mass, and dilution — and open habitat with little cover is WHY large hoofed prey such as zebras and gazelles rely mainly on grouping, alertness and speed rather than hiding (burrowers like prairie dogs can still hide underground).

activities.title: Outdoor tag: does a crowd protect the target?
steps: Play a tag game outside. Name one child the 'target zebra'; a 'lion' must tag only that named child.
Before running, predict whether the lion catches the named zebra faster when the whole herd stays clumped and milling around that child, or when that child stands alone.
Run both versions and compare how quickly the lion catches the target each time.
Discuss what the clumped, moving crowd did and, if it was harder for the lion to catch the target, why it was harder to pick out and chase one child.
activities.insight: Running both versions is intended to let children observe whether a moving, clumped crowd protects the named target, challenging the naive guess that a crowd is easy to be caught in; where the crowd does protect the target, it is because a single individual becomes hard to single out.

activities.title: Explain how the herd helps
steps: Read or listen to the scene: on the African savanna, zebras live together in big herds instead of wandering alone, and a lion is hunting nearby.
Write or say how being in a big group helps a single zebra stay safe — stating what the numbers actually DO against the predator.
Say whether the lion is a bad animal for hunting, and explain why the lion hunts at all.
Explain what it is about open grassland, rather than forest, that makes seeing danger early possible.
activities.insight: A full explanation names a mechanism — many eyes spot the predator early, or the moving crowd makes any one animal hard to single out — and treats predator–prey as feeding and survival, not malice; it links open ground to spotting danger from a distance.

activities.title: Name the cast and match who eats whom
steps: Name at least five grassland/savanna animals (e.g. zebra, wildebeest, gazelle, elephant, giraffe, lion, cheetah, hyena; bison and prairie dogs in American grasslands).
Sort the animals into plant-eaters and hunters/predators, noting that adult elephants and adult giraffes are rarely hunted, though their young can be.
Match each predator to prey it hunts (e.g. lion → zebra) to build a simple food chain.
Answer short questions on why herds help prey and on whether most hunts succeed or fail.
activities.insight: Pupils can name the savanna cast, tell apart plant-eaters and predators, describe who eats whom, and begin to flag that most hunts fail and that a big group is not an easier target.

activities.title: Open-ground scene and optional safari-guide hook
steps: Explore a savanna scene with a grazing herd and a stalking predator at a distance; tap predator and prey roles to reveal who eats whom.
Compare a 'many eyes' picture of a herd's overlapping fields of view with a lone animal's blind spots, and discuss what the herd can see that the lone animal cannot.
Look at a seasonal map showing herds moving to follow green grass and water, and say why the herds keep moving.
Optionally, hear a safari-guide-in-role describe the scene as a curiosity hook, then return to the simulation or explanation task to test the ideas raised.
activities.insight: Open sightlines across grassland with only scattered trees, overlapping herd vigilance, and seasonal movement are visible features that set up the deeper survival logic; the scene and guide spark interest but the probabilistic payoff is explored in the other activities.

checkQuestion: On the African savanna, zebras live together in big herds instead of wandering alone. A lion is hunting nearby. How does being in a big group help a single zebra stay safe?
checkAnswer: In a big herd there are many eyes and ears to spot the lion early and warn the others, and when they all run any one zebra is less likely to be the one caught — the moving crowd makes it hard for the lion to pick out and chase a single target. Safety comes from numbers, shared lookout and confusion, not from the zebras fighting the lion off.
